## **Migratory Bird & Bat Monitoring Study at the Crescent Ridge Wind Power Project, Bureau County, Illinois:  September 2005 – August 2006**

## **Executive Summary**

A post-construction bird and bat monitoring study was conducted at the Crescent Ridge Wind Power Project (hereafter “the Project”) site in Bureau County, Illinois near the town of Tiskilwa.  The study was conducted to determine the overall numbers of collision fatalities of these organisms caused by the Project.  The Project consists of 33 wind turbines, each about 120 m (~394 feet) in height and generating about 1.5 MW of energy, as well as two 50m -60m guyed meteorological towers, each about 50m to 60m (~164-197 feet) in height.  Ten of the 33 turbines were lit with FAA obstruction marking lights, seven of which were L-864 flashing red strobelike beacons and three of which were L-810 steady burning red lights.

All 33 turbines and the two meteorology towers were searched at five day intervals in Fall 2005 (September-November), Spring 2006 (March-May), and August 2006.  Searches were done out to a radius of 70 m in corn, soybean, and other agricultural fields.  During the study period, a total of 1,363 turbine (568 in Fall, 597 in Spring, 198 in August) and 84 meteorology tower searches were completed on 139 days (58 in Fall, 60 in Spring, 21 in August).  Coverage amounts to 65.0% (139 of about 214 days) of the days during which the study occurred.  This coverage amounts to 42 surveys of all 33 turbines (32 turbines in Fall 2005 – one turbine was being repaired).

The numbers of bird and bat carcasses found during the study period were relatively small.  A total of 10 bird fatalities were located along with 21 bat fatalities.  Ten species of birds and three species of bats were found.  Among the birds there were six songbirds, two waterbirds (American Coot and Yellow Rail), one raptor (Red-tailed Hawk), and no waterfowl or shorebirds.  Eight of the birds found were nocturnal migrants.  Birds found dead were all from common species.  Among the bats found, there were approximately equal numbers of silverhaired, hoary, and eastern red bats found.  These species are known as tree bats and are believed to be common migrants in the Midwest.  They are the same species that are found dead most often at other wind power facilities.  None of the bird or bat carcasses found were from species that are considered endangered, threatened, or species of special concern under either federal or Illinois state law.

Searcher efficiency and carcass removal trials were conducted in Fall 2005, Spring 2006, and August 2006 to determine the rate of carcass detection by searchers and removal of carcasses by scavengers.  The results of these trials were used to estimate upward from the number of carcasses actually found to the number that likely were there during the study period.  This estimation procedure is needed to determine the actual mortality level at the Project as well as the confidence interval for the estimates.  The procedures used for both the field and statistical components have been peer reviewed.

Including carcass removal and searcher efficiency estimates, it is likely that the total numbers of birds and bats killed during the entire Study period was about 31 birds and 93 bats. This amounts to less than 1 bird killed per turbine and about 3 bats killed per turbine during the periods August-November and March-May.  A statistical analysis of the Study’s results shows that the 95% confidence interval around the above estimates is equal to approximately 3 birds and 9 bats.  This means that with 95% likelihood, not more than about 34 birds and about 102 bats have been killed during the study period.  Actual numbers for fatalities per year could be slightly greater, based on the fact that our sampling did not include all months when bats and birds are active during the year.  However, the months in which searches were conducted represent the periods when a large majority of avian mortality has been reported from eastern and Midwestern wind power sites.

Bird and bat fatalities were greatest during September and overall numbers were greatest during September and October.  During these months seven of ten (70%) birds were found and 20 of 21 (95.2%) bats were found.  Most birds were found within about 45 m of the turbine bases, whereas most bats were found within about 30 m.

The number of birds and bats found dead under turbines lit with FAA obstruction beacons was not greater than the number found at turbines without FAA lighting.  This finding is in agreement with findings at many other wind power facilities, as well as recent studies at communication towers that have concluded that flashing L-864 red strobe-like lights do not attract night migrants.

The results of our study suggest that the search interval of five days between searches was sufficient to determine the numbers of fatalities with a high degree of confidence, especially because all turbines were searched as opposed to a subset of turbines.  Furthermore, the search area (out to 70 m) was judged to be adequate for searching under turbines, based on the rapid decline in numbers of birds and bats found beyond about 30-45 m from turbines despite the fact that searches were conducted out to 70 m.

The fatality rates and species composition of birds and bats found dead during this study are consistent with post-construction studies conducted at other wind power facilities in the United States, especially in the Midwest.  The numbers of birds and bats found dead were similar to the numbers reported from multi-year studies in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Iowa.  Bird and bat fatality numbers were slightly lower than those reported from the eastern United States. Overall, it appears that the mortality of birds and bats at the Crescent Ridge site is small and not likely to be biologically significant.  Based on the results of the monitoring program, there is nothing to suggest that either further studies or the implementation of mitigation measures are warranted.

## **1.0 Introduction**

Wind power has been touted as one of the cleanest and most benign forms of utility scale electric generation now available.  However, because avian and bat fatalities have been reported at wind power projects, post-construction impact studies are now being requested by various state and federal wildlife agencies, as well as non-profit environmental organizations.  These studies seek to determine the number and type of birds and bats killed at wind power facilities. In the more than dozen fatality impact studies that have been conducted in the Midwest and western United States, impacts to birds and bats have been minimal with, perhaps, one exception (Erickson et al. 2001; Howe et al. 2002, Johnson et al. 2002, Jain 2005).  Currently, there are no studies that permit the impacts of wind power on wildlife to be compared with conventional electric generation modes, such as coal, natural gas, nuclear, or others.  Such comparisons are necessary to evaluate the relative impacts of the various modes of commercially feasible electric generation.  Information from such studies would provide guidance for future electric generation

This report details the results of a bird and bat fatality impact study (the “Study”) at the Crescent Ridge Wind Power Project (hereafter, the “Project”) facility located near Tiskilwa, Bureau County, Illinois.  The Study was conducted during a one-year period including fall 2005, spring 2006 and August 2006.  Kerlinger (2002), who conducted a Phase I avian risk assessment for the Project, recommended that impacts to birds be studied following construction so as to provide a quantitative estimate of the numbers of flying organisms impacted by the project. Implementation of the Study is required under the Special Use Ordinances issued by Bureau County for the Project.   The Study was designed primarily to examine impacts to migrating birds and bats, a majority of which occur at the times of year listed above.  The Study was designed using methods commonly used in the wind power industry and accepted by various regulatory agencies as a means of determining the overall magnitude of collision fatalities that occur to both birds and bats.  The Illinois Department of Natural Resources (“IDNR”) and the US Fish & Wildlife Service (“USFWS”) reviewed the scope of work for the Monitoring Program, and all comments received from those agencies on the scope of work were addressed to the agencies’ satisfaction.

## **2.0 Background**

The Project consists of 33 turbines and 2 meteorology towers located in mostly corn and soy fields on flat to slightly rolling hills.  The turbines are numbered from #1 to #34; #15 does not exist.  For technical reasons, turbine #1 was being repaired during the Fall 2005 study period, so carcass searches at this tower could not be conducted.   Throughout the Fall 2005 study period, individual turbines were occasionally shut down to correct mechanical or electrical issues common during the first weeks of operation.  Those shutdowns occurred mostly during the daytime (i.e., not during times of nocturnal migration activity) and were for limited periods of time. Therefore, these shutdowns are not considered to have had a significant impact on the validity of the Study.  Each turbine is approximately 120 m (~390 feet) in height and the guyed meteorological towers are approximately 50-60 m in height.  Seven of the turbines were lit with L-864, red flashing strobe-like FAA beacons and three were lit with L-810 steady burning red lights at the top of the nacelle (about 80 m [262 feet] AGL).  Gravel and asphalt roads connect the turbines, making access relatively easy.

## **3.0 Study Area and Methods**

The detailed design of the Study is set forth in the scope of work dated August 2005, a copy of which is attached hereto as Exhibit A (the “Scope of Work”).  It covers two migration seasons (one fall and one spring) and is based on substantially similar methodologies used to study fatalities of birds and bats at wind turbine sites at many wind plants in the United States, including sites in Minnesota, Iowa and Wisconsin (Table 1.). The IDNR provided comments on the draft scope of work via a letter dated December 22, 2004.  Those comments were considered and a number of the recommendations were incorporated into the final design of the Monitoring Program.  Additional comments and questions regarding the scope of work from the IDNR and the USFWS received in December 2005 and May 2006 were addressed to the agencies’ satisfaction, as confirmed by the letter from the IDNR dated April 27, 2004 and the email from the USFWS dated July 10, 2006, copies of which are attached hereto as Exhibit B.  Because of a delay in the completion of the Project, the start of the Study was changed from July 2005, as originally planned, to late August 2005.  An additional month of searches in August 2006 was added to the final Study to ensure that data for a full fall migration season was collected.  An interim report specific to the fall 2005 field season was completed in early 2006.  The present report incorporates information from that interim report and field data from spring and August 2006.

## **3.1 Field Methods**

Carcass searches were conducted on a 5-day cycle, and required two days for each complete search when two searchers were used and 3-4 days when a single researcher conducted the work.  Search time per turbine or meteorology tower varied due to weather and ground cover conditions.

The five day interval between searches was determined to be adequate based on carcass removal times at other studies conducted at Midwestern wind power sites including those in Wisconsin (Howe et al. 2002), Iowa (Koford et al. 2005, Jain 2005), Minnesota (Johnson et al. 2002), in Michigan (Gehring and Kerlinger 2007) and elsewhere (Morrison 2002).  In Minnesota, mean carcass removal time was found to be about 7 days for birds and 10 days for bats.  In Wisconsin, carcass removal was about 16% per day, suggesting that, on average, 50% of carcasses were present on the fifth day following a fatality.  In Iowa, between 82% and 93% of carcasses remained after 2 days, suggesting that about 7% of carcasses were removed each day resulting in about 70% of carcasses being present after 5 days.  In Michigan, the mean carcass removal rate was about 6 days during about 92 trials that were conducted (Gehring and Kerlinger 2007).  Morrison (2002) reviewed some of the above project results as well as others from Oregon, California, and Vermont.  The scavenging rates at these locations were actually lower than those reported from the Midwestern sites.  All of these studies were conducted in agricultural fields, old fields, grasslands, and, or brushy fields and are the most relevant studies for evaluating the present Scope of Work.  With these rates of carcass removal and those subsequently found at the Project, five day search intervals are more than adequate for estimating overall mortality of birds and bats at the Project, especially because all turbines were searched rather than a sample of turbines.

Because of a delay in the completion of the Project, the start of the Study was moved back from July 2005, as originally planned, to late August 2005.  An additional month of searches in August 2006 was added to the final Monitoring Program to ensure that data for a full fall migration season is collected.

The combined study periods correspond to the two migration periods for birds (spring and fall) and the migration period for bats  identified at more than 15 bat fatality studies done at wind power facilities across the country (August, plus portions of September).  Note that the inclusion of late September through November and the spring period result in covering the periods during which more than 80-90% of bat fatalities have been found at wind power plants.

Three main habitat types were present underneath the turbines: corn, soybeans and fallow fields (Table1).   Crops were planted right up to the gravel circle around the base of the turbine. Table 2 summarizes the ground cover beneath the turbines searched in 2005.  For 2006, the planting patterns were similar with some rotation of soybeans to corn.  Crop (ground) cover was dense for most of the search season.

The presence of tall corn from September to mid-October in 2005 and August 2006 (see Table 2) necessitated an adaptation of the circular plot search pattern employed by the field team. Due to the height and density of the corn, standardized concentric circle searching could not be conducted during those times, mostly because rangefinders and GPS units could not consistently be relied on.  Each turbine located in a cornfield was, therefore, surveyed with a square, 140 m x 140 m grid pattern instead of concentric circles until the respective fields were harvested. Observers used rangefinders and a compass to orient themselves to walk the grids.  Broken cornstalks were used to designate the outer perimeter of the search area.  One observer would start on the outer perimeter row, and the other would start 3 rows inward from the outer perimeter observer.  A distance of three rows apart was chosen to ensure that the observers were

able to clearly see the entire search area.  Each observer would walk for approximately 10 meters then shift 3 rows over and walk for another 10 meters then shift back 3 rows to their initial starting row.

The following procedure was employed for circular search patterns.  Concentric rings were located at 15 m intervals.  The distance of each search ring from the tower was determined by using a rangefinder and each turbine / tower was searched in concentric rings out to a distance of 70 m from its base.

Data were recorded using two data sheets (Appendix I and II).  Daily search information, including weather, date, turbines / towers searched, and weather on the previous night, was recorded on a Daily Data sheet (Appendix I).  When carcasses of birds or bats were found, relevant information was recorded on the respective Carcass Data sheet (Appendix I).  For each carcass, the following information was recorded:  species (when able to be determined),

date/time, observer name, identification number (using a date and number system), turbine / tower number, distance from turbine / tower (m), cardinal direction from turbine (NW, SE, W, etc.), and condition of the migratory bird or bat carcass (scavenged, entire, partial, estimated duration of time on ground, description of remains, presence of maggots, other details regarding carcass condition).  A separate instruction sheet was developed to provide information on determining freshness of carcasses and specific information to be collected.  Any migratory bird or bat carcasses that were found were documented in place and then collected and individually placed in a plastic, zip-lock bag.  Protocols were employed to minimize direct exposure to the carcasses to insure the health of the technicians and to protect the integrity of any migratory bird or bat carcasses that were found.  The carcasses were taken to a freezer (located in a garage adjacent to the Project’s onsite operations & maintenance office) and stored for the remainder of the study period.  Most of the bat carcasses were used for searcher efficiency and scavenger removal studies and in that process were removed by scavengers.  In addition, in cases where the species of bat carcasses could not be clearly identified by the on-site researchers, final species identification was performed by Karen Tyrell, Ph.D., of BHE Environmental, Inc., an experienced bat biologist who was also a member of the Indiana Bat Recovery Team.  BHE Environmental assumed responsibility for further disposition of those carcasses.

## **3.2 Estimation of Migratory Bird and Bat Fatalities at the Project Site**

It is recognized that the number of carcasses found under the towers is lower than the total number of birds and bats likely to have been killed.  There are at least two correction factors that need to be accounted for.  The first is the possibility that the searchers will miss carcasses due to the amount of ground cover or the size and coloration of the species making it difficult to spot them.  This is called searcher efficiency.  A second possibility is that the carcasses are removed by scavengers prior to the time the searchers arrive on location after the collision event occurred. Applying these correction factors to the actual number of carcasses found during standardized surveys, provides a more realistic estimation of mortality.  Seasonal scavenger removal and searcher efficiency studies, conducted during search seasons, estimated the proportion of carcasses missed by the searchers and the proportion removed by scavengers within the 5 day search cycles.

In studies that sample a subset of the turbines present at a site, another correction must be made.  For example, if only one-quarter of all turbines are searched at a project site, the actual number of carcasses likely to have been present would  be about four times what was estimated from actual carcass numbers found, along with carcass removal and searcher efficiency corrections.  However, because all operational turbines at the Crescent Ridge site were searched, only searcher efficiency and carcass removal corrections were necessary.

We made the following adjustments to extrapolate the mortality counts to estimated mortality for the entire wind farm. We adjusted the number of carcasses found ( _C_ ) for scavenger ) removal rates ( _Sc_ ) and search efficiency ( _Se_ ) to calculate the estimated number of fatalities ( _C_ ).

Proportion of test carcasses left by scavengers within the search period ( _Sc_ ). The rate of carcasses not removed by scavengers( _Sc_ ) was measured over tests conducted in each part of the study period. In Fall 2005, 14 small birds (e.g. European Starlings) and 9 medium

sized birds (e.g. Ring-billed Gulls) were placed at various searched sites in the Project area. In Spring 2006, 24 small and 26 medium sized birds were used, and in August 2006 11 bats, 3 small and 7 medium sized birds.

Field technicians monitored carcasses daily for five days, for evidence of scavenging. The status of each carcass was reported as scavenged, partially scavenged or removed. The probability of a collision event is equally distributed over all days of the search cycle (5 days). Thus, the overall duration between carcass fall and discovery is approximately half the actual search cycle (3 days). For example, if a carcass was discovered at a 5-day search site, it had an equal probability of having hit the tower on each of the previous 5 nights. The average time between impact and discovery is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5)/5 = 3 days. Thus, the proportion of carcasses not scavenged was calculated for the number of test carcasses that were not visible (body of carcass removed/severely scavenged) after 3 days.

Proportion of carcasses missed by observers in the search efficiency trials ( _Se_ ). As described in more detail below, searcher efficiency trials were conducted for each observer by having an independent technician place bat carcasses and bird carcasses of the sizes mentioned above, under towers in the Project area, without the knowledge of the searchers. The searchers recorded all carcasses that they discovered, including carcasses planted by the independent technician. Planted evidence of collisions was later removed from the database and a mean search efficiency rate ( _Se_ ) was calculated.

## **3.3 Searcher Efficiency Study**

The objective of a searcher efficiency study was to estimate the proportion of carcasses that a searcher was able to find from the total number of carcasses that were present beneath turbines / towers.  A detection probability was calculated to estimate the total number of migratory birds and bats killed by the wind turbines when corrected for detection bias.  Three searcher efficiency tests were conducted: one in the winter (December, 2005); one in late spring (May, 2006); and, one in August 2006 for birds and bats.

Permits to salvage, possess, and transport migratory bird and bat carcasses were secured from the IDNR and the USFWS prior to the initiation of the Study.  Carcasses collected at the site which were suitable for use were used to test searcher efficiency and scavenger removal rates.  However, due to the paucity of birds found at the site, the primary source of avian carcasses used in these tests was an agency operating a government control program (USDA APHIS).

In addition to using actual carcasses, we used stuffed birds of the size and shape of those expected to be found dead under turbines (based on results of studies from Wisconsin, Iowa, and Minnesota) for the searcher efficiency studies.  A total of about a dozen artificial birds was used and mixed with actual carcasses to estimate searcher efficiency.

These avian carcasses were placed randomly beneath the wind turbines before dawn on three days of searches.  The numbers of carcasses placed at the turbines ranged from 0 to 2. Direction and distance of placement was randomly determined for each carcass prior to the searcher efficiency study.  Carcasses were tossed behind the back of the tester at each of these locations and left in the position in which they landed – an attempt to simulate carcass condition following collision of a migratory bird or bat with a wind turbine.  Test birds were discretely marked with dental floss.  Searchers were not told that they were being tested; however, searchers became aware of the test once the first test bird or bat was recovered.  The searchers recorded the direction and distance of each test bird or bat found, but test birds (excluding the artificial birds) or bats were not removed from the study site.  Instead, they remained in place for the carcass removal study.

## **3.4 Carcass Removal Study**

The objective of a carcass removal study is to determine the average length of time that a carcass remains under a turbine before removal by scavengers.  That  rate is used to adjust for removal bias when estimating the total number of carcasses present for different types/sizes of migratory birds.  Three carcass removal tests were conducted in conjunction with the searcher efficiency tests for birds and bats.  The study for bats was conducted in August 2006, the month during which most bat fatalities occur at wind turbines.

As described above, the carcasses used in the searcher efficiency study were also used in the carcass removal study.  Carcasses were to be checked 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 days after they are placed out, and were then checked during regular searches for the remainder of the season or until the carcass was removed or decomposed.   In December, 2005 the carcasses could only be

checked for the first two days due to a heavy snow fall.  Presence/absence for each carcass was recorded as well as body condition (lightly scavenged, heavily scavenged, etc).

This test permitted adjustments upwards from the actual number of carcasses found to the probable number that were on the ground before scavengers removed them.  Each carcass was individually marked and located on the ground to ensure that it was not counted as an actual fatality resulting from collisions with wind turbines or meteorology towers.

## **4.0 Results**

## **4.1 Summary of Search Effort**

During the study period, September 2005 through August 2006, a total of 42 rounds of searches at all turbines and at the two meteorology towers was conducted (Table 3; Table 4). These searches included 18 rounds in Fall 2005, 18 rounds in Spring 2006, and six rounds in August 2006.  Searches were conducted on 139 days of the 214 days that were within the study period, which translates to searches on two out of every three days (65.0%).  Spring and Fall coverage were roughly equal with 58 days spent in the field in Fall and 60 days during Spring. Another 21 days were spent in the field in August 2006.

With respect to individual turbine searches, a total of 1,363 were conducted during the study period, along with 84 searches of the two meteorology towers.  Again, coverage was roughly similar between Fall and Spring, with 568 turbine searches being done in Fall and 597 being done in Spring.  A total of 198 turbine searches were completed in August 2006. Individual meteorology tower searches total 36 in Spring, 36 in Fall, and 12 in August 2006.

Each turbine and meteorology tower was searched, on average, about every 5 days.  Searches commenced at about sunrise and continued for 7-8 hours.   The above summary does not include five additional field days during the period August 29 and September 2, 2005 during which the study areas beneath turbines were being determined and measured.  During these five days, the area beneath all turbines was also searched to determine if carcasses were present at the commencement of the study.

## **4.2 Summary of Fatalities**

## **4.2.1 Fatalities**

No carcasses were found during setup/clean-sweep in late August-early September 2005. During the entire study period (Table 4), a total of 10 bird and 21 bat carcasses were found at wind turbine sites.  No fatalities were located at the meteorology towers.  With respect to raw carcass data, one bird carcass was found for every 137 turbine searches conducted.  For bats, the comparable statistic was one bat carcass for every 65 turbines searched.  However, these numbers are not corrected for removal of carcasses by scavengers or carcasses overlooked or missed by searchers.

Bird fatalities were mostly songbirds, with six of 10 (60%) being songbirds (Table 5). There were no waterfowl or shorebirds found dead, although two waterbirds, an American Coot and a Yellow Rail were among the fatalities.  The remaining birds were one raptor (Red-tailed Hawk), and one Chimney Swift.  Eight of the individuals found were night migrants.  Not more than a single individual of any species was found dead during the Study.  Among the songbirds were species that nest in the boreal or northern temperate forest (Magnolia Warbler, Dark-eyed Junco, Golden-crowned Kinglet, and Yellow Rail).  The others could have originated in Illinois or other Midwestern states.  Those species nest in a variety of habitats, as well as being migrants or wintering birds in Illinois.

Among bats, three species were among the fatalities, and one unidentified carcass was found (Table 5).  Of the 21 carcasses, silver-haired bats were most common (38.1%), followed by equal numbers of hoary and red bats (28.6%).  These species are all considered tree bats. Their normal summer range is well to the north of Illinois, although these bats migrate through Illinois and some may winter in Illinois.

Bird and bat fatalities occurred mostly during Fall, the peak season of nocturnal autumn bird and presumably bat migration in Illinois.  During this season all but two of the bird and one of the bat fatalities were found.  Thus, 80% of bird carcasses were located in Fall.  Of these four were located during September, three in October, and one in November.  Carcasses found in Fall were mostly songbirds and migrants, whereas the two carcasses found in Spring included a Redtailed Hawk and an American Coot.  No bird carcasses were found in August.

Twenty of 21 (95.2%) bat carcasses were discovered during fall.  Fifteen (71.4%) carcasses were located in September, five (23.8%)in October, and one (4.8%) in August (Table 5).  No bat carcasses were located in November or during spring.

## **4.2.2 FAA Lights and Turbine Collision Fatalities**

Three of eight (37.5%) of night migrants that were found at turbines were at turbines deployed with FAA lighting.  This number is about what is expected by chance (30.3% of 8 total night migrant fatalities).  Ten of 33 turbines (30.3%) at the Project were equipped with FAA lights (seven with flashing red L-864 strobe-like beacons and three with L-810 steady burning red lights).  Because the numbers of fatalities were so low and because these percentages were nearly identical, there does not appear to be a difference in fatality rates between lit and unlit turbines.  In other words, carcasses were scattered throughout the wind farm and there was no suggestion that bird fatalities were clustered at turbines with FAA lights.

As with birds, FAA obstruction lights on turbines do not seem to attract migrating or foraging bats, which would result in collisions with the turbine rotors.  Two of 21 bats (9.5%) were found dead at turbines with FAA L-864 flashing red strobe-like beacons.  This number appears to be fewer than would be expected by chance (about 30.3% or 6.4 bats).

## **4.2.3  Fatality Locations**

A large majority (83.9%) of the 31 bird and bat carcasses retrieved were found within about 45 m or turbine bases (Figure 3).  Of the 31 carcasses located during three seasons of searches, 77.4% were found within 30 m of the turbine base, whereas another 16.2% was found within 31-60 m and only 6.5% were found between 61-70 m.

Bats tended to fall closer to turbines than did birds.  The mean distance of bat carcasses from turbines was 18.4 m, with a median distance of 16 m.  Nineteen of 21 (90.4%) bat carcasses were found within 26 m of the turbine base.  Only two carcasses were found beyond this distance.  One was at 41 m and the other at 59 m.  For birds, the mean distance of carcasses was 35.1 m, with a median of between 28 and 42 m.  Bird carcasses were spread over a larger distance from the turbines with 5 of 10 (50%) being within 28 m of turbines and the remaining 50% being between 42 and 68 m.

The above results strongly suggest that the search area, out to 70 m from turbine bases, is large enough to encompass most, if not all, of the area in which carcasses fall after collisions with turbines.   If the percentages shown in Figure 3 were extrapolated to the distances beyond 70 m, the figure would show very few carcasses were likely to be found beyond 70 m.  Thus, the area chosen for searching for carcasses was adequate to achieve robust statistical estimates of overall numbers of fatalities.

## **4.2.4 Listed Species**

The U.S. and Illinois lists of endangered and threatened species, as well as species that are candidate species and species that are species of special concern under Illinois law were used to evaluate the presence or potential presence and risk to these species at the Project site.   None of these birds were found to nest on the Project site or use the site other than in a transient manner (Kerlinger 2002).

Consistent with the Kerlinger (2002) report, no federally or Illinois bird or bat listed species were found during the study.  Bat species found were all common species in the United States and/or Canada, and bird species were common with the possible exception of one species found.  A single Yellow Rail was found in October 2005.  This species is relatively rare in the United States, because it generally nests at northerly latitudes (northern Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota, and Canada) and is present only as a migrant in Illinois.  There is little information on the population status of this species (Bookhout 1995).  Among the bats, all three species identified among the fatalities are relatively common bats, summering over a wide geographic range.

## **4.3 Adjusting Fatality Estimates**

The protocols for conducting the searches compare quite favorably with practices employed elsewhere.  Table 6 shows the range of frequency of the search intervals employed in

various studies and summarizes the searcher efficiency rates at other projects as well as the period of time that the carcasses tended to remain on the ground. This table shows that successful studies have been carried out where the search interval was often greater than the average number of days which the carcasses remained on site.  We did not check carcasses beyond 7 days.  If we had, the average number of days which the carcasses remained on site could have been higher than those shown below.  However, we presumed that all the carcasses that remained on the 7[th] day were scavenged on the 8[th] day (erring heavily on the side of caution).  Using that approach, the average days to scavenging was at least 5.82 days for Spring 2006 and at least 4.3 days for Fall 2006.  By using a search interval of 5 days, we detected a carcass three days after it had hit a tower, on average (see Section 3.2 above).  As the search interval used in this Study is shorter than or close to the average number of days that carcasses remain on the ground, we were able to successfully find most carcasses and correct for those carcasses already scavenged, in a manner comparable to or with greater accuracy than the studies listed in Table 6.

## **4.4 Habitat and Search Difficulty**

Corn and other vegetation made it difficult to search beneath turbines during  September and early October, 2005 (in the Fall 2005 study period), and in August 2006.  Nevertheless, in the Fall 2005 study period 22 of the 28 bird and bat carcasses (79%) were found prior to harvesting.  It is also important to note that after the corn and soybeans were harvested (from October 6 through the 25th) and before it grew to a height that made searching more difficult (June), searching was relatively easy.  Bare ground in the Spring 2006 study period (March through May) and from mid-October through November, made it much easier to search for carcasses during those months.

Although there is a high confidence level in the analysis we ran, it is possible that during September to mid-October 2005, the searcher efficiency rates could have been lower than those measured in the December, 2005 test situation.  Despite the fact that nearly 80% of the carcasses were found before the fields were harvested, to be conservative, we ran additional simulations in which we deliberately decreased searcher efficiency and increased scavenger removal to assess the impact of different rates to allay concerns arising from a) the snow-abbreviated scavenger study in Fall 2005, and b) the fact that Fall 2005 search efficiency testing occurred after vegetation was removed from sites.  For that simulation, a searcher efficiency rate of 35% test

carcasses accurately located and a scavenging rate of 55% carcasses remaining on site was applied to birds in 2005. The same search efficiency (35%) rate was applied to bats in 2005. However, since the estimated bat scavenging rate was already higher than the suggested simulation rate, we continued to use the estimated rate of 36% of bats remaining on site.  Using those assumptions, the resulting estimate of birds killed in the Fall 2005 search season would have been 43 ± 4 birds, (95% confidence interval, “CI”) or 1.3 birds/turbine.  The resulting estimate of bats killed in the Fall 2005 search season would have been 162 ± 18 bats (95% CI) or 4.91 bats/turbine.  A 95% CI means that the true estimate is 95% likely to be within the CI, (i.e. there is a 95% probability that the true estimate is between 39 and 47 birds (43 ± 4 birds, (95% CI)).  It must be emphasized, however, that these estimates are a result of a simulation where estimated rates were replaced with exaggerated, more severe rates to approximate a ‘worst-casescenario.’

## **5.0 Discussion**

## **5.1 Fatality Rates at Crescent Ridge Compared to Other Wind Power Projects in the Eastern and Midwestern United States**

Overall, small numbers of fatalities were noted during the study period at the Project, and a majority of both bird and bat fatalities were found during Fall 2005.  Very few fatalities were found during Spring 2006 and August searches.  In addition, no federally or Illinois endangered or threatened bats or birds or species of special concern were found.  All specimens were common species, with the possible exception of the one Yellow Rail carcass.  The latter species is fairly common in northerly locations, mostly in the northern Midwest and well north into Canada.  Although it may not be as common as the other species encountered, it is not in danger of becoming listed, except in farmland areas of the United States where its habitat has been decimated by farmland clearing, draining of wetlands, and mowing.

The results with respect to birds concur with statements by Kerlinger (2002) in the Phase I Avian Risk Assessment for the Crescent Ridge Wind Power Project, Bureau County, Illinois. The results also concur with testimony given by Kerlinger to the Bureau County Zoning Board in 2002.  In that report and during those hearings, Kerlinger stated that birds, including endangered and threatened species would not likely be at biologically significant risk.  That only a single individual was found of each of the ten avian species listed in Table 5 suggests that the Crescent Ridge wind power project poses no significant or undue risk to the populations of those species. The results are not dissimilar to other studies at wind turbine sites in Wisconsin, Iowa, Minnesota and other areas of the Midwest (Table 12), as well as in the Eastern United States (Table 13).

## **5.2 Seasonal Distribution of Fatalities**

The seasonality of avian fatalities at the Project were not entirely in agreement with results from previous studies.  Bird fatalities during spring migration seemed to be somewhat lower at the Project than at other facilities, whereas during fall they seemed comparable.  With respect to bats, the seasonal distribution of fatalities was in partial agreement.  Most studies have identified few bat fatalities in spring, few in late fall, and a majority of fatalities in late summer and early fall.  The results from the Project are in agreement with other studies regarding few bats being found dead in spring and late fall.  However, there were few fatalities during most of August.  It is possible that fall migration period of bats in Illinois is a bit later than at more northerly locations.  This fact would account for the fact that most bats were found in September and into October.  For example, in northeastern Wisconsin Howe et al. (2002) found that most of the bats killed were found in August and September, and many fewer were found in October. The fact that so few bats were found dead in August suggests either later migration there, overall fewer bat fatalities, or some factor that limited the numbers of bats killed during August.

## **5.3 Distance of Carcasses From Turbines and Search Area**

Recently, questions about the appropriate size of the search area beneath turbines (distance of searches from turbine base) have been asked by wildlife agency biologists and environmentalists.  By recording the distances of every carcass from turbine bases, we were able to determine that there is a declining function with respect to the number of carcasses and distance from turbines.  A majority of bird and bat carcasses were found within 30-45 m from turbines, despite the fact that searches extended out to about 70 m and greater from turbine bases.

Our results correspond closely to the results reported in mortality studies at many other wind power projects.  For example, at the Wisconsin wind power project (Howe et al. 2002), the mean distance of birds from the turbines was about 30 m and a vast majority of bats were within 40 m.  At the Mountaineer, WV, study (Kerns and Kerlinger 2004), bird carcasses were mostly within about 40 m, whereas bats averaged about 20 m and most were found between about 16 and 30 m from turbine bases.  Many other studies in the Midwest, west, and eastern states show virtually the same pattern for carcass locations in relation to distance from turbine bases.

The concurrence of our Study results for distance of carcasses from turbines at other wind power sites across the United States strongly suggests that a search area with a radius of 70 m, as was the case in our Study, is sufficient to provide a robust estimate overall fatalities of birds and bats at turbines.

## **5.4 Adequacy of Search Frequency**

The interval between carcass searches at both wind turbines and communication towers is critical for making accurate estimates of overall mortality.  There has been a discussion regarding how often searches should be done at turbines, mostly as a result of carcass removal by scavengers.  In our Study, we searched at five day intervals, which is shorter than most other studies that have been conducted to date.  Our search interval was shorter than search intervals used in peer reviewed studies such as a study at the Buffalo Ridge wind power facility in

Bird and Bat Impacts at Crescent Ridge Wind, IL

Minnesota (Johnson et al. 2002), but longer than used in studies in Wisconsin and Iowa, where searches were done every other day to every three days (in the migration seasons).

What is most important to note is that carcass removal rates are very similar among Midwestern and most other wind power sites in the United States.  For this reason, it is highly likely that the search frequency of five days that we used is more than adequate, especially because we searched all turbines rather than a subset of turbines.  The fact that all turbines were searched increases our confidence that our estimates are robust.  In most other studies, subsets of turbines (sometimes 30% - Jain 2005, Iowa DNR and Iowa State University) are searched, thereby reducing confidence in overall estimates.  From our low scavenging rate and searches of all turbines we are confident that our results are robust and close estimates of the fatality rates that are actually occurring at the project turbines.

## **5.5 Habitat and Search Difficulty**

Although there is a high confidence level in the analysis we ran, it is possible that during September to mid-October (when corn and other vegetation made it difficult to search beneath turbines), the searcher efficiency rates could have been lower than those measured in the December, 2005 test situation.  Despite the fact that nearly 80% of the carcasses were found before the fields were harvested, to be conservative, we ran additional simulations in which we deliberately decreased searcher efficiency and increased scavenger removal to assess the impact of different rates.  As we discussed above, even using exaggerated rates of scavenger removal and searcher inefficiency, the per turbine fatality rates for birds and bats would have fallen well within the range of fatality rates projected at other locations (Tables 12 and 13.)

## **5.6 No Further Studies Warranted**

Based on the results of the monitoring program, neither further studies nor the implementation of mitigation measures are warranted.
